description_full: D.R. Horton, Inc. operates as a homebuilding company in East, North, Southeast, South Central, Southwest, and Northwest regions in the United States. It engages in the acquisition and development of land; and construction and sale of residential homes in 126 markets across 36 states under the names of D.R. Horton. The company also constructs and sells single-family detached homes; and attached homes, such as townhomes and duplexes. In addition, it provides mortgage financing and title agency services; and engages in the residential lot development business. Further, the company develops, constructs, owns, leases, and sells multi-family and single-family rental properties; conducts insurance-related operations; and owns water rights and other water-related assets, as well as non-residential real estate, including ranch land and improvements. It primarily serves homebuyers. D.R. Horton, Inc. was founded in 1978 and is headquartered in Arlington, Texas.

financial_summary: D.R. Horton, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $39.5B market cap on $34.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 9% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $3.3B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.95× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 12.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 11% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.
